title: Computational Thinking & Programming Logic
description: Learn to reason about inputs, variables, control flow, functions, collections, algorithms, edge cases, and correctness before asking AI for code.

lessons.title: Input, process, and output
lessons.principle: An algorithm accepts defined inputs, performs finite steps, and produces observable results or errors.
lessons.practice: Explain a tip calculator as input amount and rate, a calculation, and displayed total.

lessons.title: Trace a simple calculation
lessons.principle: Manually tracing values reveals hidden assumptions about units and rounding.
lessons.practice: For 100 currency units with a 10 percent tip, record intermediate values and the expected 110 total.

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.principle: Variables name values; types determine valid operations and representations.
lessons.practice: Distinguish numbers, strings, booleans, null, and collections in a simple form.

lessons.title: Avoid string-number confusion
lessons.principle: Form inputs may arrive as text even when users typed numeric characters.
lessons.practice: Convert intentionally and reject non-finite or invalid input before arithmetic.

lessons.title: Expressions and operators
lessons.principle: Expressions combine values using arithmetic, comparison, and logical rules.
lessons.practice: Use parentheses to make important conditions unambiguous.

lessons.title: Respect boolean precedence
lessons.principle: A complex condition can grant access accidentally when AND and OR are mixed.
lessons.practice: Write a truth table for 'is owner OR is editor AND resource is public' and clarify intended grouping.

lessons.title: Conditions and branches
lessons.principle: Conditional logic chooses behavior based on explicit predicates.
lessons.practice: List mutually exclusive cases before writing if/else or match logic.

lessons.title: Handle the default path
lessons.principle: An omitted else branch can silently return undefined or leave stale state.
lessons.practice: Specify the result for unknown statuses and invalid enum values.

lessons.title: Loops and termination
lessons.principle: Repeated work needs clear iteration bounds and an exit condition.
lessons.practice: Trace a loop over three tasks and identify which elements are included.

lessons.title: Avoid off-by-one errors
lessons.principle: Using an inclusive boundary instead of an exclusive one can skip or overrun elements.
lessons.practice: Test zero, one, and last-element cases for an indexed loop.

lessons.title: Functions and parameters
lessons.principle: Functions package behavior behind a name, inputs, return value, and side-effect contract.
lessons.practice: Write small functions with one responsibility and named parameters.

lessons.title: Separate pure logic from I/O
lessons.principle: Pure functions return the same output for the same inputs and are easier to test.
lessons.practice: Move price calculation outside the DOM event handler so AI-generated UI changes cannot alter the rule.

lessons.title: Arrays, objects, and maps
lessons.principle: Collections model ordered items, structured records, or keyed lookup with different semantics.
lessons.practice: Choose an array for ordered tasks and an object for a task's fields.

lessons.title: Choose identifiers deliberately
lessons.principle: Array position is not a durable identifier when items can be reordered or deleted.
lessons.practice: Give each saved task a stable ID and use it for updates and event correlation.

lessons.title: Algorithms and pseudocode
lessons.principle: Pseudocode expresses an approach independently of programming-language syntax.
lessons.practice: Describe a search/filter operation in plain steps before implementing it.

lessons.title: Check algorithm invariants
lessons.principle: An invariant is a condition that must remain true through each iteration.
lessons.practice: When filtering tasks, ensure every emitted result matched the predicate and preserved expected order.

lessons.title: Boundaries and invalid inputs
lessons.principle: Correctness includes empty data, missing values, duplicates, and very large or malformed inputs.
lessons.practice: Build a test table with nominal, edge, and invalid cases.

lessons.title: AI-generated code needs counterexamples
lessons.principle: A helpful model can still write code that only succeeds on its demonstration input.
lessons.practice: Challenge it with empty arrays, duplicate IDs, negative values, and unexpected types.

lessons.title: Complexity and clarity
lessons.principle: Time and memory use increase with input size; clear correct code usually comes before optimization.
lessons.practice: Recognize linear search and nested-loop growth without premature micro-optimizing.

lessons.title: Measure before optimizing
lessons.principle: A faster-looking alternative may introduce worse complexity, allocations, or maintenance cost.
lessons.practice: Benchmark representative input sizes and preserve correctness tests while changing an algorithm.
